Name: query_gated_retrieval
Title: Same Fact, Different Roads: Query-Phrasing Determines the Retrieval Circuit
Short Hypothesis: A single stored fact is retrieved through partially distinct circuits depending on how the query is phrased (cloze vs question vs translation vs multiple-choice), such that component ablations that break one phrasing leave others intact. Understanding this query-dependence is essential to explain why models 'know' a fact under one prompt but not another.
Related Work: Prompt-sensitivity of factual recall is documented behaviorally (Elazar et al., 2021, consistency; Jiang et al., 2020, LAMA prompts) but not mechanistically decomposed. Causal tracing studies typically fix a single cloze template. We go further by mapping, for the SAME fact, how the causal circuit shifts across phrasings, distinguishing shared storage from phrasing-specific access pathways.
Abstract: Language models are notoriously inconsistent: a fact recalled from one prompt may vanish under a paraphrase. We ask whether this reflects distinct retrieval circuits keyed to query form rather than distinct storage. Holding the underlying (subject, relation, object) triple fixed, we render each fact under multiple query formats and perform path patching and component ablation to identify the attention heads and MLP modules causally responsible in each. We hypothesize a shared mid-layer storage locus at the subject position but format-specific access pathways-notably different attention heads that move the retrieved attribute to the answer position for questions versus cloze completions. We predict that ablating a format-specific head degrades that format while sparing others, and that facts which are behaviorally inconsistent across formats correspond to those with the least overlapping circuits. We quantify circuit overlap with a Jaccard-style measure over causally-implicated components and correlate it with behavioral consistency. This reframes prompt inconsistency as an access problem: the knowledge is stored once but reached through fragile, phrasing-specific routes. The findings suggest that improving factual reliability may require strengthening or unifying access pathways rather than adding storage, and that consistency benchmarks measure circuit convergence rather than knowledge presence.
Experiments: 1. Build a set of facts, each rendered in 4 formats (cloze, natural question, multiple-choice, cross-lingual). 2. For each fact-format pair, run path patching from a corrupted to clean run to identify causally-important heads/MLPs; record component sets. 3. Compute circuit-overlap (Jaccard) across formats per fact. 4. Measure behavioral consistency (agreement of answers across formats). 5. Correlate overlap with consistency. 6. Validate by ablating a format-specific head and confirming selective degradation. Metrics: per-format circuit sets, circuit-overlap score, consistency-overlap correlation, ablation selectivity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Path patching is compute-intensive and sensitive to the choice of corruption. Distinguishing 'shared storage, different access' from 'different storage' requires careful shared-node analysis. Formats differ in token structure, confounding circuit identity. Results may not generalize across relations.
